What should I know first?

Six ideas worth carrying into every consultation.

These are the highest-priority ideas across the three issues—not a substitute for the full notes below.

  1. 01
    Pattern before promise.

    Food processing, meal timing and macronutrient labels are useful lenses, but no single label tells the whole health story.

  2. 02
    Ask before you advise.

    When a client struggles, explore barriers, preferences, readiness and plan fit instead of assuming a knowledge or discipline problem.

  3. 03
    Match the claim to the design.

    A cohort can identify an association; a short trial can test a narrow outcome. Neither answers every clinical question.

  4. 04
    Scope is an active skill.

    Membership, a webinar, a symptom tool or laboratory access never replaces competence, consent, collaboration or referral.

  5. 05
    Make progress visible.

    Track energy, confidence, symptoms, skills and follow-through—not only weight—and be clear that subjective ratings are not diagnoses.

  6. 06
    Build the system before the extras.

    A reliable intake, interaction screen, referral path, documentation rhythm and follow-up process come before more services.

Client-counselling toolkit

Language that keeps the client in the conversation.

Use these as adaptable prompts, not a script to perform. Listen to the answer before deciding what comes next.

Scope cue

“That question sits outside my training. I’d like you to discuss it with your physician, pharmacist or another appropriately regulated provider.”

When follow-through is hard
“What has made this difficult?”

Find the barrier before changing the recommendation.

When the plan does not fit
“What would make it easier?”

Invite context: time, cost, culture, symptoms, confidence or enjoyment.

When confidence is low
“What is one change you feel confident trying this week?”

Scale the experiment until success feels plausible.

When priorities drift
“Would it be okay if we revisit what matters most to you?”

Return to the client’s own reason for change.

When you disagree
“Can you tell me more about that?”

Curiosity creates room for correction without defensiveness.

When emotion arrives
“That sounds really discouraging. We can pause.”

Validation is not agreement; it is recognition of the experience.

Evidence check · October 21, 2026

Read the claim. Then read its boundary.

Labels apply to the specific claim shown—not to an entire article, person or practice approach.

SupportedPromising but limitedAssociation onlyOpinion / practice suggestionRequires verificationNot supported as stated

Practice-building reference

Build a practice that is clear, useful and honest about the work.

The business articles are suggestions, not promises. Count preparation, administration, follow-up, privacy obligations and costs whenever you evaluate a service.

  1. 01

    Foundation

    Define scope, intake, consent, privacy, documentation, interaction screening and referral paths.

  2. 02

    Workflow

    Batch administration, protect focused work, use templates appropriately and leave 10–15 minute appointment buffers.

  3. 03

    Useful visibility

    Offer accurate education, community talks and memorable follow-ups without diagnosing or implying endorsement.

  4. 04

    Service design

    Describe the components and support included in a program. Never guarantee a health result or insurer reimbursement.

  5. 05

    Measurement

    Track revenue per total hour, retention and recurring work alongside quality, boundaries and client experience.

10 things to remember

Your one-page mental model.

Read this before returning to the longer notes, then use the recall prompts to test what stayed with you.

  1. 01

    Ultra-processed food is a useful research category, but foods and dietary patterns within it are heterogeneous.

  2. 02

    One short controlled trial can show causation under its conditions; it cannot prove a lifetime outcome.

  3. 03

    Relative risk is not a percentage-point change in one client’s absolute risk.

  4. 04

    A non-significant result is not proof that two approaches are equivalent.

  5. 05

    “Low carbohydrate” is incomplete until you know what replaces the carbohydrate.

  6. 06

    Five daily fruit-and-vegetable servings was an observed mortality plateau—not a maximum or individual prescription.

  7. 07

    Cell and animal findings can be promising without being a human treatment recommendation.

  8. 08

    Listening, validation and collaborative experiments usually teach you more than the label “non-compliant.”

  9. 09

    A database warning signals a risk to investigate; it does not diagnose a nutrient deficiency.

  10. 10

    Membership benefits, tools and testimonials do not expand scope or establish clinical effectiveness.
